E0157.summary: Writer of L’Antiquitie devoilee par ses Usages, cited by Atwood critically for treating the Mysteries as a depository of the religious melancholy of the first men.
E0157.body: Atwood cites the author of *L’Antiquitie devoilee par ses Usages, etc.* only to criticize him: he saw the Mysteries as a depository of the religious melancholy of the first men, a view Atwood rejects [II.2 ¶4; II.2 n4].

forms: the author of the Filum Ariadne
E0158.summary: Writer of Le Filet d’Aridane, cited in support of the point that the dissolution needs hands, which Nature lacks.
E0158.body: Cited (work: *Le Filet d’Aridane*) in support of Atwood’s point that the dissolution requires hands, which Nature lacks: “Nature cannot of herself enter into the dissolution” [IV.1 ¶5; IV.1 n3]. Atwood endorses the citation.

E0159.summary: Writer of the Lucerna Salis (cited in Digby’s translation), repeatedly used by Atwood in support of points on the white work, prayer and labour, the gold of the Wise, and fermentation.
E0159.body:
Atwood cites the *Lucerna Salis* (footnoted as Digby’s translation / Digby’s *Lucerna Salis*) several times, always in support:

- **White work**: on the whitening of the matter, with the advice “Govern your fire with a great deal of care” [III.2 ¶5; III.2 ¶6; III.2 n7].
- **Study, prayer and labour**: study, meditation and prayer are needed; God grants the art only through instruction and labour, and without prayer obstructs or spoils it: “He does not either grant it immediately to any person, but always by mediate dispositions, to wit, by instructions and the labour of the hands” [III.4 ¶20; III.4 n21]. Also cited for many passages to the same effect as Ricardus [III.4 n16].
- **Gold of the Wise**: from the Latin verse *Aurum Sapientum*, the gold of the Wise as pure water, its dissolution and reunion into One inseparable Thing; it declares “the gold of the Wise to be by no means vulgar gold” [III.3 ¶32; III.3 n22].
- **Fermentation and multiplication** (cap. 8): fermenting with pure gold or silver before projection, purifying the metals, and tenfold multiplication by dissolving and coagulating; “one drachm of gold is sufficient for the fermentation in the red” [IV.3 ¶24; IV.3 n5].

forms: author of the Lumen de Lumine
E0160.summary: Writer of the Lumen de Lumine, cited from its chapter on Matter in support of Atwood’s account of Tenebrae activae beneath sense and imagination.
E0160.body: Cited from the chapter on Matter in *Lumen de Lumine* in support of Atwood’s account of the *Tenebrae activae* lying beneath sense and imagination, described as “a certain horrible, inexpressible chasm” [III.2 ¶13; III.2 n13].

forms: the wise author of the Rosarium
E0161.summary: Writer of the Rosarium, cited by Atwood in support of solution, dissolution and patient repetition, and among testimonies to inexhaustible abundance she says are not literally true.
E0161.body:
Atwood cites the *Rosarium* (Rosar. Abbrev., Tract ii, De Lapide, in Thet. Chem., vol iii) in support of Solution as the first preparation: subjects of species must be reduced to first matter, with an analogy from glass-making [I.2 ¶5; I.2 n2].

It also supports dissolution, the earthy body of sense made to flow: “Corpora qui vult purgare oportet fluxa facere” [II.3 n2] (ours: whoever would purge bodies must make them fluid).

The “wise author of the Rosarium” (cap. 3) is cited for grinding, cooking and repeating without weariness: “Tere, coque, et reitera, et non te taedeat” [IV.1 ¶7; IV.1 n7].

As “Author of the Rosary” he is cited for an inexhaustible abundance won by industry, patience and one’s own labour, in a passage that continues with Eirenaeus and is footnoted to *Introitus Apertus* cap. 35; Atwood then says this testimony is not literally true [IV.3 ¶26; IV.3 n7].

E0162.summary: Unnamed authorities cited in support of the claim that the three terms of adoration contain all the Divine measures.
E0162.body: Cited, unnamed, in support of the statement that the three terms of adoration contain all the Divine measures [III.4 ¶25].

E0163.summary: In Atwood’s words the first and last defect, leading either to fruitless search in inert matter or, in Mammon’s followers, to abuse of attained power.
E0163.body: Atwood calls it “this first and last defect of Avarice” [III.4 ¶4]. It leads either to fruitless searching in inert matter or, among the followers of Mammon, to abuse of the power once attained [III.4 ¶4].

E0164.summary: Named by Atwood as demanding notice, with nothing further said.
E0164.body: Named as demanding notice; the text says nothing more about him [I.1 ¶35].

E0165.summary: Reputed practitioner of transmutation, cited by Atwood on species and the Matter and named among masters who wrote obscurely.
E0165.body:
Atwood lists works attributed to him (*de Tinctura Metallorum*, *Porta Elementa*, *de Mineralibus*) and calls him a reputed practitioner of transmutation and magic whose writings are neither lucid nor numerous [I.1 ¶35; I.1 n40]. He is cited, by reference only, as concurring on species [I.2 ¶5; I.2 n5], and as one of the Mahomedan princes who agreed concerning the Matter [III.2 ¶60].

In Norton’s verse “Avicen” is named among masters who wrote obscurely: “Wrote under coverts and Aristotle alsoe.” [I.1 ¶15]. Within the *Ordinal* his *Porta* is cited for balanced feeding of the matter: “Comedas ut bibas, et bibas ut comeda;” [IV.1 ¶12] (ours: eat as you drink, and drink as you eat).

E0166.summary: Name for the Universal Mercury and the Stone’s active principle, which with fire suffices for the work, reducing bodies to First Matter and reanimating them.
E0166.body:
Khunrath (quoted) identifies it: “Azoth, viz., the Universal Mercury” — “which alone with its internal and external fire is sufficient for thee”, transforming itself by fire into what it will, and visible and tangible [I.1 ¶81]. Elsewhere Khunrath presents it as something to be touched and seen, sufficient with internal and external fire for the Stone: “thou shalt see Azoth! The Universal!” [III.3 ¶9].

The Latin formula “Ignis et Azoth tibi sufficient” is given as Hermes’ saying via Norton, without explanation [IV.2 ¶13] (ours: fire and Azoth suffice for thee). In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer) Atwood repeats it as sufficient for the freed spirit: “ignis et Azoth tibi sufficient” [APP ¶131].

In IV.3 a cited voice (“continues he”) makes it the Stone’s active principle: “Azoth of our Stone, continues he, reduces bodies to their First Matter and reanimates them with the Universal Form” [IV.3 ¶28]. The vivific Ens is so named because it adheres to bodies, drawing its like into itself by supernatural magnetism: “the Hermetic philosophers have given it the name of azoth, which adheres to bodies” [IV.3 ¶29].

Asserted identities: = Universal Mercury [I.1 ¶81]; = The Universal [III.3 ¶9]; = vivific Ens [IV.3 ¶29].

E0167.summary: Named among masters who celebrated the Head Stone and wrote obscurely; his dictum on man as Nature’s servant is accepted by Atwood only for outward seeking.
E0167.body:
In Norton’s verse Bacon is named among masters who wrote obscurely: “Wrote under coverts and Aristotle alsoe.” [I.1 ¶15]. He is named as celebrating the Head Stone [III.1 ¶21], and as having observed the Organon becoming worse than useless [III.2 ¶42].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer) Atwood uses his lucid style to show that clear language seems mystical when turned to the a priori ground [APP ¶111]. She accepts his dictum “Man is the servant and interpreter of Nature” only for outward seeking and qualifies it: turned within, man can be Nature’s revealer and master [APP ¶120].

E0168.summary: Cited as illustration: his ass was clear-sighted and spoke.
E0168.body: Used as an illustration: Balaam’s ass was clear-sighted and spoke [III.2 ¶64].

forms: the bards and hallowed sages of Asia Minor
E0169.summary: Ancient sages contrasted with moderns: they knew their Creator under the same sun under which moderns remain blind.
E0169.body: Atwood contrasts them with moderns: they knew their Creator under the same sun, while moderns remain blind [IV.4 ¶28].

E0170.summary: Adept called “the monk”, praised by Atwood as the star of his century and among her most-cited authorities on First Matter, Antimony, extraction, and experience before practice.
E0170.body:
Atwood praises Basil Valentine as the star of the fifteenth century, credited with a new method for the Red Elixir, and assesses editions and translations of his works (*Chimische Schriften*, *Triumphal Chariot of Antimony*, *Stone of Fire*, *Twelve Keys*) [I.1 ¶59; I.1 ¶61; I.1 n65]. He is listed among genuine seekers against the spurious brood of idlers [I.1 ¶49], among adepts warning against practice before full understanding, though “Basil’s” receipts also misled literal readers [I.1 ¶86], and as agreeing concerning the Matter [III.2 ¶60].

**First Matter.** From *De Prima Materia*: it is like no particular thing, indescribable without experience, one yet three, a third thing: “Corpus anima spiritus in duobus existit” [I.2 ¶31; I.2 ¶32; I.2 ¶42; I.2 n33] (ours: body, soul, spirit exist in two). All metals have one root containing mercury, salt and sulfur: “all metals and minerals have one root from whence their descent is” [II.1 ¶11; II.1 n8]. His *Stone of Fire* allegory of flight, fall and mountain Atwood reads as displaying the whole metaphysico-chemical analysis; it names what “is the first matter of all things” [III.2 ¶19; III.2 ¶20; III.2 n20].

**Antimony and extraction.** The true tincture is not common antimony; “how that extraction should be made, is a principal secret in which the whole art of Alchemy consists” [II.1 ¶25]. “in the preparation of Antimony consists the Key of Alchemy”, done with the microcosm’s corporeal fire [III.1 ¶37; III.1 n42]. Antimony must be freed of venom, which Atwood glosses as purging self-will from the mind; separation is by Fire, Vulcan the sole master: “Our Antimony, says Basil Valentine, which is fixed, searcheth out fixed diseases” [IV.1 ¶40; IV.1 n34].

**Experience.** “Learn and look for the first foundation, says the monk, which nature holds concealed” — advice Atwood calls excellent; his celestial part, separating pure from impure by spiritual reason, leads into her turn to spiritual reason [III.1 ¶13; III.1 n10; III.1 n14; III.1 n15]. “more is learned by once seeing the work done, than can be taught by the writing of many pages” [IV.1 ¶2; IV.1 n1]. The winged Matter must be bound and accustomed to flight gradually, lest like Icarus it fly too near the Sun: “permit it not to fly suddenly” [IV.1 ¶15; IV.1 n15].

He also teaches that exterior spirits are intelligent and deceive the unwary, being “endowed with senses and understanding, know Arts, and have in themselves an occult operative life” [II.3 ¶23; II.3 n18]. In the Appendix (later layer) his *Keys* are called the best illustration of the Art as a fermentative process [APP ¶29].

E0171.summary: In Eudoxus’ words, the spirits of the bodies, where Sun and Moon wash; the King’s bath, prepared with the blood of the Innocents, in which he is made young.
E0171.body: Eudoxus (quoted) identifies the bath with the spirits of the bodies: “the spirits of the bodies are the Bath where the Sun and Moon go to wash themselves” [IV.3 ¶10]. One must “prepare the bath of the King with the blood of the Innocents” [IV.3 ¶10], and “purify, to heal, and to animate the royal bath” [IV.3 ¶16], in which the King is made young again. Asserted identity: = the spirits of the bodies [IV.3 ¶10].

E0172.summary: In Atwood’s account, a bath prepared out of the blood of many battles, preceding the rising of the Identical Spirit.
E0172.body: Atwood: “So the Bath of Diana is prepared out of the blood of many battles” [III.1 ¶68]; it precedes the rising of the Identical Spirit [III.1 ¶68].

E0173.summary: That which is referred to all things and through which they sympathize, inconceivable by ordinary reason, which the soul enters after descent to nonentity.
E0173.body: Atwood: Being cannot be conceived by ordinary rational contemplation; “it becomes necessary simply to refer Being to all things, and all things sympathize thereby internally with each other” [III.2 ¶50]. The soul becomes into it after its descent to nonentity, and one is present with it by being present with oneself: “then he is present with true Being, which is everywhere” [III.2 ¶59].

E0175.summary: Voice in the Turba Philosophoru, cited by Atwood to explain the paradox of the ‘stone and no stone’.
E0175.body: Cited from the *Turba Philosophoru*, Sermo Vigesima (the classic synod of Aristaeus), in support of the paradox of ‘stone and no stone’: “this very permanent water is the stone, but whilst it is water it is no stone” [I.2 ¶29; I.2 n31].

E0176.summary: Phrase of the masters which Atwood applies to the matter’s ripened Life; it is unclear whether it names the green or the purple colour.
E0176.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer) Atwood writes: “The purple color is its ripened Life; it is the benedicta viriditas of the masters” [APP ¶119] (ours: blessed greenness). Since the passage joins green and purple, which colour the phrase names is unclear.

E0177.summary: Voice cited via Vaughan’s Coelum Terrae in support of solve et coagula, the gross body as vessel, heavenly fire, and work without tools.
E0177.body: Cited (footnoted to Mehung in Vaughan’s *Coelum Terrae*, p. 122) in support of solve et coagula, the gross body as the vessel, the heavenly fire, and work without tools: “For I have my heavenly fire, which excites and stirs up the elemental one” [III.3 ¶24; III.3 n14].

forms: the best Greek Authors, historical and philosophic
E0178.summary: Greek historical and philosophic writers whom Atwood invokes as giving collateral probability to alchemy’s antiquity.
E0178.body: Invoked as providing collateral probability for the antiquity of alchemy [I.1 ¶3].

E0179.summary: Cited in the Appendix: its protest against idolatry applied to self-made specificating, and Revelation said to rectify man and Nature.
E0179.body: Both references are in the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer). Atwood applies the Bible’s protest against idolatry to unlawful specificating from one’s own mind [APP ¶37]. Revelation rectifies man and Nature; the question of science versus the Bible is left on its own ground [APP ¶161].

E0180.summary: Collection whose second edition Atwood notes as containing the Twelve Keys.
E0180.body: Its second edition is noted as containing the Twelve Keys [I.1 ¶61].

E0181.summary: Twofold conception, which Atwood says must be rejected for Nature to reach Monadic simplicity.
E0181.body: Atwood: Nature reaches Monadic simplicity “through the rejection of the Binary” [IV.2 ¶18], “by rejection of her Binary conception” [IV.2 ¶20]. The context suggests it means a twofold conception.

E0182.summary: Cited from Siris in support of a universal material called ether, source of air’s vitalizing power.
E0182.body: Cited from *Siris* in support of a universal material called ether, the source of the air’s vitalizing power, “a pure invisible fire” [I.2 ¶14].

E0183.summary: Cited in the Appendix for Nature being as much God’s voice as Revelation; Atwood agrees, then qualifies that since the fall Nature distorts it.
E0183.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer): “Nature, as the Bishop of Oxford (Wilberforce) says, is as much the voice of God as Revelation is” [APP ¶161]. Atwood agrees, then qualifies: since the fall Nature distorts that voice [APP ¶161].

E0184.summary: Stigmatizing name given to alchemy, perhaps derived from Chemia meaning black matters.
E0184.body: Atwood notes that alchemy “has been likewise stigmatized as a Black Art” [I.1 ¶5], perhaps from Chemia taken to mean black matters [I.1 ¶5].

E0185.summary: The adepts’ name for the dark nether region and the apparent corruption preceding mystical death and regeneration.
E0185.body: Atwood: “It is the Black Saturn of the adepts, and that appearing corruption that precedes the mystical death and regeneration into new life” [II.3 ¶18]; it names the dark nether region. Asserted identities: = lapis niger — “as describing the same ens, they call it lapis niger, vilis, foetens” (ours: black, vile, stinking stone) [II.3 ¶18]; = Urinus Saturni — “Sendivogius calls it Urinus Saturni” [II.3 ¶18].

E0186.summary: In Eudoxus’ words, the source of the black, foul, stinking fume whose separation forms the white Stone.
E0186.body: Eudoxus (quoted) speaks of “the black, foul, and stinking fume of the Blackest Black” [IV.3 ¶3], whose separation forms the white Stone.

E0189.summary: Read variously by quoted authorities: in Roger Bacon’s phrase the understanding; in verse from Theat. Chem. Brit. the principal matter of all that increases; in Boehme the fire-and-water union whose warmth is life.
E0189.body:
The records give three quoted readings, not reconciled:

- **Roger Bacon**: blood = the understanding: “operate according to the blood; i.e., according to the understanding” [I.1 ¶86].
- **Verse in Theat. Chem. Brit.**: blood contains the three things and the nature of gold, has the proportion of the four elements, and is the principal matter of everything that increases: “For blood is the principle matter of each thing” [II.1 ¶15].
- **Jacob Boehme**: the red fire-form and the thin water-form, “both of which contracting together into one, are converted into Blood”; “the original in the blood, viz., fire, which is its warmth, is life”, and from that warmth the Thin Water of Life proceeds [III.3 ¶24].
